---
title: "Exposure offsets"
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

A count depends on the opportunity to observe events. Ten liaison tokens in one thousand words and ten liaison tokens in one million words describe very different rates. The amount of opportunity is called **exposure**. In Nettle's data, country area is a proposed exposure because larger countries provide more geographic space in which languages are recorded. Recall that the [country count](poisson-regression.qmd#nettle-country-counts) is a geopolitical database total, so whether area functions as exposure is an assumption that we must inspect.

An **offset** is a predictor whose coefficient is fixed in advance rather than estimated. In a Poisson model with a log link, entering log exposure as an offset fixes its coefficient at one. The algebra below shows that this is exactly the claim that expected count equals exposure times an expected rate.

An offset fixes a scientifically meaningful coefficient rather than estimating
it. We derive that constraint from an area-rate equation so that its consequences
for the fitted country count remain visible.

```{r}
#| label: load-nettle-offset
#| echo: true
nettle <- read.csv("data/nettle/nettle-1999-climate.csv")
stopifnot(nrow(nettle) == 74L)
```

If $A_i$ is area and $r_i$ is the expected language rate per unit area, then

$$
\lambda_i=A_i r_i,
$$

so

$$
\log\lambda_i=\log A_i+\log r_i
=\log A_i+\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{MGS}_i.
$$

The offset is $\log A_i$ with coefficient fixed at one.

That fixed coefficient makes a strong proportionality claim. Holding growing season fixed, two otherwise identical countries with areas $A$ and $2A$ have

$$
\frac{\lambda(2A)}{\lambda(A)}
=\frac{2A\exp\{\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{MGS}\}}
{A\exp\{\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{MGS}\}}=2.
$$

An offset model thus says twice the area implies twice the expected reported country total. Calling area “opportunity” does not make this proportionality automatic; it remains a substantive claim about geopolitical database counts. A free area model replaces the fixed one by $\gamma\log A_i$; an ordinary area covariate on the unlogged scale instead assumes $\log\lambda_i$ changes linearly per square kilometer. These are different scientific claims.

```{r}
#| label: derive-and-fit-offset
#| echo: true
nettle$derived_log_area <- log(10) * nettle$log10_area_km2
stopifnot(max(abs(nettle$derived_log_area - nettle$log_area_km2)) < 1e-10)
fit <- glm(language_count ~ mean_growing_season_months + offset(derived_log_area),
           poisson(link = "log"), nettle)
free_area <- glm(language_count ~ mean_growing_season_months + derived_log_area,
                 poisson(link = "log"), nettle)
raw_area <- exp(nettle$derived_log_area)
area_covariate <- glm(language_count ~ mean_growing_season_months + raw_area,
                      poisson(link = "log"), nettle)
nettle$fitted_count <- predict(fit, type = "response")
head(nettle[c("country", "language_count", "fitted_count")])
```

```{r}
#| label: compare-area-specifications
#| echo: true
data.frame(model = c("log-area offset", "estimated log-area coefficient",
                     "raw-area covariate"),
           area_coefficient = c(1, coef(free_area)["derived_log_area"],
                                coef(area_covariate)["raw_area"]))
```

```{r}
#| label: offset-count-plot
#| echo: true
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(nettle, aes(language_count, fitted_count)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "grey65", linewidth = .5) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5, color = "#1F5A85") +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Observed language count", y = "Fitted language count") +
  theme_classic()
```

The teaching table's `Area` column is base-10 logarithmic. A Poisson log link uses natural logarithms, hence the explicit conversion $\log A_i=\log(10)\log_{10}A_i$. Treating area as exposure assumes proportionality between expected count and area. Nettle instead estimates the area coefficient. We fix it at one here to examine the consequences of proportional exposure, while retaining the fitted coefficient specification as a live alternative.[^nettle-teaching-table]

[^nettle-teaching-table]: The transformed table comes from Bodo Winter's [course data](https://github.com/bodowinter/applied_statistics_book_data). Nettle's appendix reports area in square kilometers; the teaching table stores its base-ten logarithm.

Changing area units does not change the rate ratio for growing season: multiplying every $A_i$ by a constant adds that constant's logarithm to the offset and shifts the intercept. But using `log10(A)` without multiplying by $\log(10)$ changes the fixed exposure coefficient and hence changes the model.

## Recap and check

1. Is “twice the area means twice the expected languages” scientifically defensible here? The offset model imposes that assumption. The data alone do not. Comparing the model with an estimated area coefficient makes the assumption inspectable.
2. Why must the offset use natural logs? `glm(..., family = poisson(link = "log"))` uses the natural-log linear predictor.

We now use the [Nettle association](poisson-regression-example.qmd) to carry the offset model through interpretation and model criticism.
